notes.front: What is Projects on GitHub?
notes.back: An adaptable table, board and roadmap that integrates with your issues and pull requests to plan and track work.
notes.explanation: It works at the user or organization level, and you can filter, sort, group and chart the items it holds.
notes.example: Like a shared spreadsheet of a team's work, except each row is a live issue or pull request that updates itself.
notes.evidence: A project is an adaptable table, board, and roadmap that integrates with your issues and pull requests on GitHub to help you plan and track your work effectively at the user or organization level.

notes.front: What is the table layout in Projects?
notes.back: A spreadsheet-like view of a project's issues, pull requests and draft issues, with their GitHub metadata and custom fields.
notes.explanation: You can group, sort and filter items, and show or hide fields, to suit everyone on the team.
notes.example: Like a spreadsheet where each row is a piece of work and each column is something you track about it.
notes.evidence: The table layout is a powerful and adaptable spreadsheet comprised of your issues, pull requests, and draft issues with metadata from GitHub and the custom fields you've added to your project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Changing the layout of a view”, “About the table layout”

notes.front: What is the board layout in Projects?
notes.back: A view that spreads a project's issues, pull requests and draft issues across customisable columns.
notes.explanation: Setting the column field to a "Status" field turns it into a kanban board.
notes.example: Like sticky notes on a wall under the headings To do, Doing and Done.
notes.evidence: The board layout spreads your issues, pull requests, and draft issues across customizable columns. You can create a kanban board by setting your column field to a "Status" field
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Changing the layout of a view”, “About the board layout”

notes.front: What is the roadmap layout in Projects?
notes.back: A high-level timeline view of a project across a configurable timespan, where you can drag items to change their dates or iteration.
notes.explanation: It lets you track work over time and watch progress.
notes.example: Like a wall planner with bars stretching across the weeks each job should take.
notes.evidence: The roadmap layout provides a high-level visualization of your project across a configurable timespan, and allows you to drag items to affect their start and target dates or selected iteration.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Changing the layout of a view”, “About the roadmap layout”

notes.front: What is a custom field in Projects?
notes.back: Metadata you add to a project's issues, pull requests and draft issues, beyond the built-in metadata.
notes.explanation: Custom fields build a richer view of item attributes; you are not limited to built-in metadata such as assignee, milestone and labels.
notes.example: Like adding your own column, such as "Effort", to a shared to-do spreadsheet.
notes.evidence: You can use custom fields to add metadata to your issues, pull requests, and draft issues and build a richer view of item attributes. You’re not limited to the built-in metadata (assignee, milestone, labels, etc.) that currently exists for issues and pull requests.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Projects”, “Adding metadata to your items”

notes.front: What is a draft issue, in Projects?
notes.back: A project item for quickly capturing an idea; it exists only in your project and can be converted into a regular issue later.
notes.explanation: Unlike issues and pull requests, it is not stored in a repository, so it needs converting to an issue before it can have labels or a milestone.
notes.example: Like a pencilled note on a planning board, sitting among the typed-up tickets.
notes.evidence: Draft issues are useful to quickly capture ideas. Unlike issues and pull requests that are referenced from your repositories, draft issues exist only in your project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Adding items to your project”, “Creating draft issues”

notes.front: What is a label on GitHub?
notes.back: A tag you create to categorise issues, pull requests and discussions in a repository.
notes.explanation: Labels are one way to manage your work on GitHub, by sorting items into categories.
notes.example: Like coloured stickers on folders marking which ones are urgent and which are paperwork.
notes.evidence: You can manage your work on GitHub by creating labels to categorize issues, pull requests, and discussions.

notes.front: What is a milestone on GitHub?
notes.back: A way to track progress on a group of issues or pull requests in a repository.
notes.explanation: You create a milestone and then associate issues and pull requests with it.
notes.example: Like a checklist headed "Ready for the spring launch", with a date and a tally of what is finished.
notes.evidence: You can use milestones to track progress on groups of issues or pull requests in a repository.

notes.front: What is a built-in automation in Projects?
notes.back: A built-in workflow that updates the Status of project items when certain events happen.
notes.explanation: For example, it can set the status to Todo when an item is added, or to Done when an issue is closed.
notes.example: Like a to-do app that ticks a task off by itself the moment the related job is finished.
notes.evidence: Projects includes built-in workflows that you can use to update the Status of items based on certain events.

notes.front: What is a project template?
notes.back: A pre-configured project shared with others in your organization, for them to use as the base of their own projects.
notes.explanation: You can create one for the organization or set an existing project as a template.
notes.example: Like a blank planning spreadsheet with the columns already set up, handed to every new team.
notes.evidence: You can create project templates for your organization, or set a project as a template, to share a pre-configured project with other people in your organization which they can then use as the base for their projects.

notes.front: What is a status update in Projects?
notes.back: A high-level overview you share so people can tell the project's current state, with a status such as "On track" or "At risk".
notes.explanation: It can also carry start and target dates and a message formatted with Markdown.
notes.example: Like a traffic-light note pinned to the front of a team's plan each week.
notes.evidence: You can set a status, such as "On track" or "At risk", to allow people to quickly determine the current state of the project. You can also set start dates and target dates.

notes.front: What is a saved reply on GitHub?
notes.back: A reusable response you create for issues and pull requests.
notes.explanation: The docs suggest making saved replies for the responses you use most often, to save time.
notes.example: Like an email signature or canned answer you drop into a message with one click.
notes.evidence: Saved replies allow you to create a reusable response to issues and pull requests. Save time by creating a saved reply for the responses you use most frequently.

notes.front: What is an assignee on an issue or pull request?
notes.back: A person assigned to it, which makes clear who is working on it.
notes.explanation: You can assign several people to one issue or pull request.
notes.example: Like writing a colleague's initials on a job card so everyone knows it is theirs.
notes.evidence: Assignees clarify who is working on specific issues and pull requests.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Assigning issues and pull requests to other GitHub users”

notes.front: What are insights for Projects?
notes.back: Charts you view, create and customise that use the items in your project as their source data.
notes.explanation: You can filter the default chart or build your own, choosing the filters, chart type and information shown.
notes.example: Like a chart tab in a spreadsheet that redraws itself from the rows of work.
notes.evidence: You can use insights for Projects to view, create, and customize charts that use the items added to your project as their source data.

notes.front: What are the three layout options for a view in Projects?
notes.back: Table, board and roadmap.
notes.explanation: The docs describe them as a high-density table, a kanban board and a timeline-style roadmap.
notes.evidence: You can view your project as a high-density table layout, as a kanban board, or a timeline-style roadmap.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Projects”, “Viewing your project from different perspectives”

notes.front: You change the assignee of an issue inside a project. What happens to the issue itself?
notes.back: The issue shows the change too: the integration works both ways.
notes.explanation: Projects are built from the issues and pull requests you add, and information syncs automatically in both directions.
notes.evidence: This integration works both ways, so that when you change information about a pull request or issue in your project, the pull request or issue reflects that information. For example, change an assignee in your project and that change is shown in your issue.

notes.front: In the board layout, which kinds of field can you set as the column field?
notes.back: A "Status" field (for a kanban board), or any other single select or iteration field.
notes.explanation: The column field decides which columns the board's items are spread across.
notes.evidence: You can create a kanban board by setting your column field to a "Status" field or set any other single select or iteration field as the column field.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Changing the layout of a view”, “About the board layout”

notes.front: On a board whose column field is Status, you drag an item from the "In progress" column to the "Done" column. What happens to the item's Status?
notes.back: It changes to Done, matching the column you dragged it to.
notes.explanation: You can drag one item or several at once.
notes.evidence: You can drag individual or multiple items from column to column and the value of those items will adjust to match the column you drag them to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Changing the layout of a view”, “About the board layout”

notes.front: What does the roadmap layout use to place items on its timeline?
notes.back: Your custom date and iteration fields.
notes.explanation: These fields position issues, pull requests and draft issues on the timeline so you can track work over time.
notes.evidence: Roadmaps use your custom date and iteration fields to position your issues, pull requests, and draft issues on a timeline, allowing you to track work over time and watch progress.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Changing the layout of a view”, “About the roadmap layout”

notes.front: In the roadmap layout, what are two kinds of key date you can mark with vertical lines?
notes.back: Any two of: iterations, milestones, the dates of items in your project.
notes.explanation: The markers give an overview of upcoming workload and how it is spread across iterations.
notes.evidence: You can also display vertical lines to highlight key dates for your project, including iterations, milestones, and the dates of items in your project.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Changing the layout of a view”, “About the roadmap layout”

notes.front: A project can have up to {{c1::50}} fields, counting built-in metadata and custom fields together.
notes.explanation: The limit counts built-in fields as well, not only the ones you add.
notes.evidence: You can use up to 50 fields in a project, including built-in metadata and custom fields.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Projects”, “Adding metadata to your items”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: A team wants every item in its project to show whether it is Low, Medium or High priority. Which type of custom field fits best?
notes.back: Single select field.
notes.explanation: The docs give tracking Low, Medium or High priority as the example use of a single select field.

choicesExplained.Text field: The docs give a text field for adding a quick note, not for choosing from fixed options.
choicesExplained.Number field: The docs give a number field for tracking the complexity of a task.
choicesExplained.Iteration field: The docs give an iteration field for planning work week by week.

notes.evidence: A single select field to track whether a task is Low, Medium, or High priority.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Projects”, “Adding metadata to your items”

notes.front: Which type of custom field lets you plan work week by week, with support for breaks?
notes.back: An iteration field.
notes.explanation: Iteration fields can also serve as board columns and as roadmap positions.
notes.evidence: An iteration field to plan work week-by-week, including support for breaks.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Projects”, “Adding metadata to your items”

notes.front: You delete a label in one repository. What happens to a label with the same name in another repository?
notes.back: Nothing: adding, changing or deleting labels in one repository has no effect on other repositories.
notes.explanation: A label belongs to the repository it was created in and can be used on any issue, pull request or discussion there.
notes.evidence: Once a label exists, you can use the label on any issue, pull request, or discussion within that repository. Addition, modification, or deletion of labels in one repository has no effect on labels belonging to other repositories.

notes.front: What happens to GitHub's default labels in a new repository, and can you change them?
notes.back: They are included when the repository is created, and you can edit or delete them later.
notes.explanation: The defaults help create a standard workflow; organization owners can also customise them for their organization's repositories.
notes.evidence: Default labels are included in every new repository when the repository is created, but you can edit or delete the labels later.

notes.front: Which default label indicates a new feature request?
notes.back: enhancement
notes.explanation: GitHub's table of default labels describes `enhancement` as indicating new feature requests.
notes.evidence: enhancement Indicates new feature requests

notes.front: An issue can't be acted on until its author explains which browser they used. Which default label fits?
notes.back: question
notes.explanation: `question` indicates that an issue, pull request or discussion needs more information.

choicesExplained.invalid: `invalid` indicates the item is no longer relevant, not that it needs more detail.
choicesExplained.duplicate: `duplicate` indicates similar issues, pull requests or discussions already exist.
choicesExplained.bug: `bug` indicates an unexpected problem or unintended behaviour; it says nothing about missing information.

notes.evidence: question Indicates that an issue, pull request, or discussion needs more information

notes.front: What are two things you can see on a milestone's page?
notes.back: Any two of: its description, its due date, its completion percentage, the number and list of open and closed issues and pull requests.
notes.explanation: From the same page you can also edit the milestone and create new issues that are associated with it by default.
notes.evidence: The milestone's due date * The milestone's completion percentage * The number of open and closed issues and pull requests associated with the milestone * A list of the open and closed issues and pull requests associated with the milestone Additionally, you can edit the milestone from the milestone page

notes.front: A team wants one place showing the due date and completion percentage for the issues it must finish before a release. What should it create in the repository?
notes.back: A milestone.
notes.explanation: A milestone groups issues or pull requests, and its page shows the due date and completion percentage.

choicesExplained.A label: A label categorises items but has no due date or completion percentage.
choicesExplained.A saved reply: A saved reply is reusable text for responding to issues and pull requests.
choicesExplained.A custom field: A custom field adds metadata to project items; it does not report a completion percentage.

notes.evidence: The milestone's due date * The milestone's completion percentage

notes.front: A pull request in a newly created project is merged, and nobody has changed the project's workflows. What status does the item get?
notes.back: Done: merging a pull request sets its status to Done by default.
notes.explanation: Two workflows are on by default: closed issues or pull requests are set to Done, and merged pull requests are set to Done.
notes.evidence: When your project initializes, two workflows are enabled by default: When issues or pull requests in your project are closed, their status is set to **Done**, and when pull requests in your project are merged, their status is set to **Done**

notes.front: Which configured workflows does a project template leave out?
notes.back: Auto-add workflows.
notes.explanation: A template otherwise carries the views, custom fields, draft issues and their fields, configured workflows and insights.
notes.evidence: Project templates include the views, custom fields, draft issues and associated fields, configured workflows (except any auto-add workflows), and insights.

notes.front: What are saved replies tied to, and where can you use them?
notes.back: Your personal account; you can use them across repositories and organizations, in issues, pull requests and discussions.
notes.explanation: They belong to your account, not to a repository, and the docs list issues, pull requests and discussions as places to use them.
notes.evidence: Once you've added a saved reply, it can be used in issues, pull requests, and discussions. Saved replies are tied to your personal account. Once they're created, you'll be able to use them across repositories and organizations.

notes.front: You can create a maximum of {{c1::100}} saved replies.
notes.explanation: At the limit, you can delete saved replies you no longer use or edit existing ones.
notes.evidence: You can create a maximum of 100 saved replies. If you've reached the maximum limit, you can delete saved replies that you no longer use or edit existing saved replies.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: A maintainer spots an issue that repeats one already open and wants to mark it so, without writing her own text. What can she use?
notes.back: The GitHub-provided "Duplicate issue" saved reply.
notes.explanation: GitHub supplies this saved reply to mark an issue as a duplicate and track it with a similar issue.

choicesExplained.A milestone: A milestone tracks progress on a group of issues; it does not mark duplicates.
choicesExplained.A custom field: A custom field adds project metadata; it does not reply on the issue.
choicesExplained.A built-in automation: Built-in automations update the Status of project items based on events.

notes.evidence: You can also use the GitHub-provided "Duplicate issue" saved reply to mark an issue as a duplicate and track it with a similar issue.

notes.front: Sam has no write access to a repository but has commented on one of its issues. Can Sam be assigned to that issue?
notes.back: Yes: anyone who has commented on the issue can be assigned to it.
notes.explanation: The docs list yourself, commenters, people with write permissions and organization members with read permissions as people you can assign.
notes.evidence: You can assign multiple people to each issue or pull request, including: yourself, anyone who has commented on the issue or pull request, anyone with write permissions to the repository, and organization members with read permissions to the repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Assigning issues and pull requests to other GitHub users”, “About issue and pull request assignees”

notes.front: A team wants to assign all twelve of its members to one pull request. What will happen?
notes.back: Only up to 10 can be assigned.
notes.explanation: Issues and pull requests both support up to 10 assignees.
notes.evidence: Both issues and pull requests support up to 10 assignees.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Assigning issues and pull requests to other GitHub users”, “About issue and pull request assignees”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date
choices: Only up to 10 can be assigned
Only one person can be assigned
Only people with write access can be assigned

choicesExplained.All twelve can be assigned: Twelve is over the limit of 10 assignees.
choicesExplained.Only one person can be assigned: You can assign multiple people to each issue or pull request.
choicesExplained.Only people with write access can be ass: Commenters and organization members with read permissions can also be assigned.

notes.front: A team archives twenty finished items from its project. Will its insights charts still count them?
notes.back: No: insights does not track items you have archived or deleted.
notes.explanation: Charts are built from the items in the project, and archived or deleted ones are left out.
notes.evidence: Insights does not track items you have archived or deleted.

notes.front: How do you make a chart in insights a historical chart?
notes.back: Set the chart's X-axis to "Time".
notes.explanation: Historical charts track changes to the state of project items over time.
notes.evidence: To create a historical chart, set your chart's X-axis to "Time."
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”, “About historical charts”

notes.front: A lead wants a chart showing how much of the project's work has been completed over the past months and how much is left. Which default chart suits her?
choices: A current chart of items per assignee
notes.back: The "Burn up" historical chart.
notes.explanation: The default "Burn up" chart shows progress over time: how much work is completed and how much is left.

choicesExplained.A current chart of items per assignee: A current chart shows the present state of items, not their change over time.
choicesExplained.A milestone page: A milestone page shows a completion percentage for one group of work, not a chart over time.
choicesExplained.The board layout: The board layout arranges items in columns; it is not a chart.

notes.evidence: The default "Burn up" chart allows you to visualize the progress of your issues over time, showing how much work is completed and how much is left to do.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”, “About historical charts”

notes.front: A manager wants to see the next quarter's work laid out along a timeline and to drag items to change their target dates. Which layout should she choose?
notes.back: Roadmap layout.
notes.explanation: The roadmap layout shows the project across a configurable timespan and lets you drag items to change their start and target dates.

choicesExplained.Board layout: The board layout spreads items across columns, not along a timeline.
choicesExplained.Table layout: The table layout is a spreadsheet of items and fields, not a timeline.
choicesExplained.Insights: Insights builds charts from project data; you do not drag items there to reschedule them.

notes.evidence: The roadmap layout provides a high-level visualization of your project across a configurable timespan, and allows you to drag items to affect their start and target dates or selected iteration.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Changing the layout of a view”, “About the roadmap layout”

notes.front: A project lead wants everyone browsing projects to see at a glance that hers is "At risk". What should she post?
notes.back: A status update.
notes.explanation: Status updates set a status such as "At risk" and appear in the project's header and in lists when people browse projects.

choicesExplained.A label: A label categorises issues, pull requests and discussions, not a whole project.
choicesExplained.A saved reply: A saved reply is reusable text for issues and pull requests.
choicesExplained.A milestone: A milestone tracks progress on a group of issues or pull requests in a repository.

notes.evidence: Status updates are found on your project's side panel, below the description and README, and in the project's header and in lists when you're browsing projects.

notes.front: What is the difference between a current chart and a historical chart in insights?
notes.back: A current chart shows project items as they are now; a historical chart shows how their state changed over time.
notes.explanation: For example, a current chart can count items per person, while a historical chart tracks open, completed and not-planned items over time.
notes.evidence: You can create current charts to visualize your project items. For example, you can create charts to show how many items are assigned to each individual
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”, “About current charts”

notes.front: How does a label differ from a milestone?
notes.back: A label categorises issues, pull requests and discussions; a milestone tracks progress on a group of issues or pull requests, with a due date.
notes.explanation: The milestone page shows a due date and a completion percentage, which a label does not have.
notes.evidence: You can use milestones to track progress on groups of issues or pull requests in a repository.
